notes:
Task and constraints: Identify which receptor receives a light ray reflected inside a square room, given side length p and vertical rise q per horizontal travel.
Idea: Find the least common multiple of p and q and inspect the parity of the number of vertical and horizontal traversals.
Technique and why it applies: Unfolding reflections turns the path into a straight line. The LCM represents the first common boundary alignment; even/odd counts identify the receptor.
Invariant: L//q and L//p count vertical and horizontal segment multiples at the first alignment.
Edge cases: lcm is used without importing it. p and q are assumed positive, with q no greater than p as in the problem.
Complexity: Computing the LCM and parity checks takes O(log min(p,q)) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Determine which receptor a reflected ray reaches in a square room.
Idea: Compute the LCM of p and q, then use the parity of horizontal and vertical extension counts.
Technique and why it applies: Unfolding the room converts reflections into straight travel. The parities of lcm/p and lcm/q distinguish the three receptor corners.
Invariant: lcm is the first distance at which both wall dimensions align with the unfolded ray.
Edge cases: p and q must be positive. The local gcd routine terminates by Euclid's algorithm and avoids needing a library import.
Complexity: GCD and LCM calculation take O(log min(p,q)) time and O(1) extra space.

Task and constraints: Find the receptor hit by a ray reflecting inside a square with side p and vertical offset q.
Idea: Compare the lowest set-bit values of p and q to determine parity relationships.
Technique and why it applies: p & -p extracts the least significant set bit; comparing these powers of two identifies which factor has the extra power-of-two divisibility that determines the receptor.
Invariant: The comparison summarizes the relative powers of two dividing p and q.
Edge cases: Positive integer p and q are assumed. The nested conditional returns receptor 2, 0, or 1 according to the comparison.
Complexity: Bit operations and comparisons take O(1) time and O(1) space for bounded integer values.

Task and constraints: Check whether two equal-length strings can become equal by swapping exactly two characters in s.
Idea: Record differing positions; accept either exactly two cross-matching differences or identical strings containing a repeated character.
Technique and why it applies: Two mismatches must reverse each other's characters. If strings already match, swapping equal characters leaves s unchanged, requiring a duplicate.
Invariant: diffCharactersInS and diffCharactersInGoal hold corresponding characters at every mismatch.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths fail immediately. Counter handles repeated characters; strings with no duplicate cannot be swapped without changing their content.
Complexity: One scan and a frequency count take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether A can be made equal to B by one swap of two characters in A.
Idea: Collect at most two mismatched character pairs and handle the identical-string case separately.
Technique and why it applies: Two mismatches must be exact reversals of one another. With no mismatches, a duplicate character permits a swap that leaves the string unchanged.
Invariant: diff contains only the first two mismatch pairs; a third mismatch returns False immediately.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths fail. itertools is imported but unused.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) mismatch storage, plus O(n) space for the set used in the identical case.

Task and constraints: Determine whether each lemonade customer can receive correct change when paying with 5, 10, or 20.
Idea: Track the available five- and ten-dollar bills and greedily make change for each transaction.
Technique and why it applies: A ten requires one five; a twenty prefers one ten plus one five, otherwise three fives. This preserves fives when possible for future tens.
Invariant: five and ten count the bills available after all customers processed so far.
Edge cases: Any unsupported bill value reaches the failure branch. The method returns False as soon as the required change cannot be made.
Complexity: Each bill is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Check whether a sequence of lemonade sales can be served with exact change.
Idea: Maintain counts of five- and ten-dollar bills and apply the preferred change-making rule for each customer.
Technique and why it applies: A ten consumes one five. A twenty consumes a ten and five when available, otherwise three fives; if neither is possible, the method fails.
Invariant: five and ten reflect the inventory left after the processed bills.
Edge cases: The final else treats any non-5/non-10 bill as a twenty, which relies on the problem's allowed denominations.
Complexity: A single scan takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Decide whether lemonade transactions can be completed with correct change.
Idea: Store counts of bill denominations and greedily use the largest available change bills.
Technique and why it applies: For each customer, the code adds the payment, computes change relative to a five-dollar bill, then consumes 20, 10, and 5 denominations.
Invariant: counts stores the inventory by denomination after adding the current payment and dispensing change.
Edge cases: The approach can incorrectly use the current 20-dollar payment as available change before validating the transaction, and coins contains 20,10,5 while the loop greedily consumes values.
Complexity: Each customer may scan three denominations, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Maximize the binary score of a matrix by flipping rows and columns.
Idea: Treat each row's first bit as a row flip and calculate each column's best possible number of ones.
Technique and why it applies: XOR with A[r][0] effectively makes the leading bit one in every row. For each column, max(col,R-col) chooses whether flipping that column yields more ones, weighted by its binary place value.
Invariant: col counts ones in the column after the implicit row flips.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty rectangular matrix. The first column contributes R ones after row normalization.
Complexity: Each cell is inspected once, giving O(RC) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest contiguous subarray with sum at least K, allowing negative numbers.
Idea: Build prefix sums and maintain their indices in a monotonic increasing deque.
Technique and why it applies: If the current prefix exceeds the oldest prefix by at least K, a qualifying subarray is found. Removing larger/equal tail prefixes preserves only candidates that can lead to shorter future subarrays.
Invariant: Prefix sums at indices in monoq are strictly increasing, and their indices are increasing.
Edge cases: deque is used without import in the snippet. The algorithm returns -1 when no qualifying subarray exists.
Complexity: Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum length of a subarray whose sum is at least K, even with negative values.
Idea: Compute prefix sums and use a monotonic increasing deque of candidate prefix indices.
Technique and why it applies: A current prefix can pair with the deque front when their difference reaches K; that front is then removed because any later endpoint gives a longer subarray. Dominated tail prefixes are removed when the current prefix is no larger.
Invariant: The deque stores indices with strictly increasing prefix sums.
Edge cases: Empty arrays return -1 because no candidate is found. Negative values are supported by the prefix-sum/deque method.
Complexity: The linear scan performs amortized O(1) deque operations per index, so time and space are O(n).

Task and constraints: Find the shortest path from the starting cell to collect every key in a grid with locks and walls.
Idea: Run BFS over positions and the set of collected keys.
Technique and why it applies: Each move has unit cost, so breadth-first search finds the minimum number of steps. A state includes its key string, and locks block movement until the matching lowercase key has been collected.
Invariant: visited stores position/key combinations already expanded; steps is the current BFS distance.
Edge cases: deque is used without importing it. Counting keys by occurrences can overcount if a key letter appears in multiple cells; the usual grid constraints use distinct key letters.
Complexity: The state space is O(RC·2^K), with O(RC·2^K) time and space.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum number of steps needed to collect all keys in a maze.
Idea: Precompute shortest distances between special cells, then run Dijkstra over the current key bitmask and special-cell location.
Technique and why it applies: Grid BFS finds distances between starts, keys, and locks while treating walls as blocked. The second search adds a key bit when visiting it and permits a lock only when its bit is held.
Invariant: best[place][state] is the shortest distance found for that special location and collected-key mask.
Edge cases: The target mask assumes key letters map contiguously from a through the number of keys; gaps in key letters can make the mask incorrect. The BFS condition for recording special cells is subtle and should be checked.
Complexity: Precomputation is O(RC·S), and Dijkstra explores location-mask states with heap overhead; worst-case state space is exponential in key count.

Task and constraints: Find the smallest prime palindrome greater than or equal to N.
Idea: Generate odd-length palindromes from their first half and test each candidate for primality.
Technique and why it applies: Every even-length palindrome is divisible by 11, so only 11 needs special handling among small candidates and the search can focus on odd lengths. is_prime checks odd divisors through the square root.
Invariant: Each generated j is a palindrome and candidates are considered in increasing half-prefix order.
Edge cases: The loop ends at 10^5 for the half-prefix, so sufficiently large N may exhaust the loop and return None. The special case 8 through 11 returns 11.
Complexity: Each candidate primality test costs O(sqrt(j)) worst case; the search can be large, with O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the transpose of a matrix, swapping its row and column coordinates.
Idea: Allocate a result with reversed dimensions and copy each value to result[c][r].
Technique and why it applies: Matrix transposition maps element A[r][c] to result[c][r], so each source cell is visited once.
Invariant: After processing a cell, its value is stored at the corresponding transposed coordinates.
Edge cases: The code assumes A is nonempty because it reads A[0]. Rectangular matrices are handled by allocating len(A[0]) rows of len(A) columns.
Complexity: Time and output space are O(RC).

Task and constraints: Find the largest distance between consecutive set bits in the binary representation of n.
Idea: Scan the binary string after its leading prefix and track positions of one bits.
Technique and why it applies: Each new one defines a gap from the previous one, and the maximum gap is updated.
Invariant: prev stores the number of processed binary characters since the last one, in the code's sliced indexing.
Edge cases: bin(n)[3:] drops the first two characters rather than just the 0b prefix, so it can miss the first set bit and produce incorrect gaps. Values with few set bits return zero.
Complexity: Binary conversion and scan take O(log n) time and O(log n) string space.

Task and constraints: Compute the maximum distance between adjacent set bits in the binary representation of N.
Idea: Examine each of the lowest 32 bit positions and remember the index of the previous one bit.
Technique and why it applies: The distance between two one-bit indices is the difference in their bit positions; taking the maximum gives the binary gap.
Invariant: last is the most recent set-bit position found, and result is the largest gap so far.
Edge cases: The fixed 32-iteration loop assumes nonnegative values within 32 bits. If fewer than two bits are set, result remains zero.
Complexity: The loop takes O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space under the 32-bit constraint.

Task and constraints: Reorder nums1 to maximize the number of positions where its value exceeds the corresponding value in nums2.
Idea: Sort nums1, process nums2 from largest to smallest, and assign the largest winning value or sacrifice the smallest value.
Technique and why it applies: A maximum opponent value is matched with the smallest nums1 value that can beat it; if none can, the smallest available value is sacrificed.
Invariant: l and r delimit the unused values in sorted nums1, and ans records assignments by original nums2 index.
Edge cases: heapq is used without import. The code assumes both arrays have equal lengths; ties are treated as losses because the comparison is strict.
Complexity: Sorting nums2 indirectly via heap takes O(n log n), and assignments are O(n), with O(n) heap/output storage.

Task and constraints: Maximize the number of wins in Advantage Shuffle by permuting A against B.
Idea: Sort both arrays, assign each A value to beat the smallest remaining B value it can exceed, and save other values for losses.
Technique and why it applies: candidates groups winning values by the B value they can beat; unused small values go into others and are used where no win is possible.
Invariant: Each processed A value is either assigned to one B threshold or stored as a sacrifice.
Edge cases: candidates is keyed by B values, so repeated equal B values share one list; popping still assigns a distinct stored A value each time.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), and mapping/assignment is O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of refueling stops needed to reach target t with initial fuel F and stations S.
Idea: Sweep stations in position order, using a max-heap of fuel capacities from stations already passed whenever more fuel is needed.
Technique and why it applies: The largest available prior fuel amount gives the greatest range per stop. Each station's fuel is added to the heap after confirming it can be reached.
Invariant: The heap contains negated fuel amounts of reachable stations not yet selected, and ans counts chosen stops.
Edge cases: The method appends the target as a zero-fuel station, mutating S. It assumes stations are already sorted by position and uses heapq without import.
Complexity: Sorting is not performed; given sorted stations, heap operations give O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
